dok_rationale: Part (c) selects a bin width for the coach's question, explains how grouping changes the reader's impression, and bounds conclusions from unlabeled observations.
stem: Suppose a student recorded steps for 30 days. Histograms F and C show the same data with 1-thousand- and 5-thousand-step bins. A coach asks, ``Does this student move differently on school days and weekends?''\par\smallskip \textbf{Priya:} ``Use C. F has too many short and empty bars; C gives the clearer summary.''\par \textbf{Leo:} ``Use F. C combines values that should not be treated as one group.''
first_take: Which histogram is more useful to the coach, F or C? Name one visible feature.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State each bin width and the number of days in F's 19--20-thousand interval.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: In two sentences, describe where F's days are grouped and where its empty intervals are. Use thousands of steps.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Choose Priya's or Leo's display for a first look at the coach's question. Cite one feature that the other display hides and explain how that changes the impression. What information would you still need to tell school days from weekends?

answers.a: F uses 1-thousand-step bins; C uses 5-thousand-step bins. F has 1 day in 19--20 thousand.
answers.b: There are 21 days in the 5--9-thousand-step intervals and 8 in the 11--14-thousand intervals. No days fall in 9--11 or 14--19 thousand; one day falls in 19--20 thousand. The histogram does not show exact individual values.
answers.c: Leo's F preserves the empty 9--11-thousand interval between two groups. C merges the groups into adjacent broad bars, which could hide two possible routines. Neither graph labels the days; the coach needs the school-day/weekend label for each observation before identifying either group.

expectedElements.description: Chooses F and cites the 9--11-thousand gap or separated groups
Explains how C's broad bins can hide two possible routines
Requires school-day/weekend labels before attributing groups to day types

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: Saying F contains more observations although both show the same 30 days
Assigning a cluster to weekends without day labels
Saying narrower bins are always better instead of matching the question

The other display could make a reader think \blank[2in]. To tell which days are weekends, I still need \blank[2in].
